description:
Black Carpenter Ant (Camponotus pennsylvanicus)

16 July 2014: Observed on Cooper Creek next to Avondale Park in Denton, Texas that a rather large (one-half inch or longer) Black Carpenter Ant (Camponotus pennsylvanicus) had just come across the recently expired body of a Honey Bee on the halfway dried up creek bed. We photographed what was surely to have been a long process of harvesting the Honey Bee's body for the collective as there were any number of similarly large Black Carpenter Ants combing through the creek's bed for bits of food. We did not stay to watch them conduct the work of taking apart the Honey Bee's body but believe this is likely what occurred. The Black Carpenter Ant was at least as large as the Honey Bee if not larger. Few resources go to waste in Nature perhaps and certainly on this day we witnessed one such instance with Black Carpenter Ants and Honey Bee. Avondale Park and Cooper Creek are administered by the City of Denton, Texas.

description: Ants live in every continent except Antarctica. Camponotus vicinus is part Of the Kingdom Animalia, which is the animal kingdom. They are in the phylum Arthropoda, which includes insects, arachnids, myriapods, and crustaceans. Arthropods are characterized by their jointed limbs and cuticle made of chitin. The arthropod body plan consists of segments, each with a pair of appendages. They are in the class Insecta, which are characterized by a three-part body (head, thorax and abdomen), three pairs of jointed legs, compound eyes and one pair of antennae. They are in the order Hymenoptera, which is the third-largest order of insects, comprising the sawflies, wasps, bees, and ants. Lastly, they are a part of the family Formicidae, the ant family. Easily identified by their elbowed antennae. Camponotus vicinus is a large ant with queens being around 14-16mm, workers being around 11-13mm, miners being around 7-8.5mm, and males being around 8-11mm. They are a 1 node ant and have a 12 segmented antennae. They are normally black on their head and abdomen and red on their thorax and legs. They have many standing hairs on their whole body. Except their head, where they have only a few if any. Camponotus vicinus is unlike other carpenter ants in this area. I will compare Camponotus vicinus to Camponotus Modoc, which is different type of carpenter and in the same geographic area. Although it has black thorax instead of red. They both can have red legs and black heads and thorax. They are easy to tell apart, because of Camponotus modoc’s larger size, different coloration and much larger mandibles. Camponotus vicinus usually lives under stones and has smaller mandibles to dig in soil more often. While Camponotus modoc has much larger mandible that it used to chew through wood to make its nests. They are roughly the same size but I do believe that Camponotus modoc is usually larger just based on my personal observations. Next, Camponotus vicinus is different from other ants that aren’t part of the genus Camponotus.  Such as Pheidole megacephala, which is a much smaller and that is not a carpenter and. This ant actually has two nodes and can be red on all parts of its body. It is the same color throughout its whole body but can be black, brown, or red. This and has an abnormally large head to dig deep elaborate tunnels. Although this and does not chew through wood. It has an 11 segmented. This ant is also much smaller then Camponotus vicinus and usually has more ants in its colonies to make up for size. All three of these ants eat insects and other dead invertebrates, they will also eat honeydew which is produced by aphids. Now, Camponotus vicinus has stages to its reproduction. Although unlike some other ants, it performs all stages of reproduction year round. It has 4 main stages to development, egg, larva, pupa, and adult. They are also one of the species where pupa develop a cocoon to develop into adults. First males will fertilize eggs produced by the queen. The eggs will then hatch into larva. Larva then eat and grow into pupa. When Larva are grown enough they go into a cocoon to grow and develop into adults. This species was collected at Devils Gulch Trail Head. It was found at a north aspect under stones and in a rotten log nearby. It was a bunch grass canyon land habitat. GPS:45.5W 116.9W This species appears to have adapted smaller mandibles for better digging in soil. While still keeping them big and sharp enough to easily chew through wood. It also has seemed to have grown larger than most ants over time like most other carpenter ants. It has a stocky structures body designed to be strong unlike some other ants who are more narrow and faster. I would guess this ants would prefer to fight its enemies instead of run because of its build and its large powerful mandibles which it can use for a weapon. This ant has adapted very specifically for what it does best and has one way of life. With every ant having its own specific job to make the colony function.

Subfamily Formicinae 
Genus Camponotus (Carpenter Ants) 
No Taxon  (Subgenus Camponotus) 
Species modoc ((Western) black carpenter ant) 


Other Common Names 

Known simply as the black carpenter ant in the Mountain West and Pacific Northwest, I suggest prefacing with "Western" to distinguish from C. pennsylvanicus.

Range 
Mountains of western US and southwestern Canada (apparently nowhere sympatric with the closely related C. pennsylvanicus)

Habitat 
Conifer forest, in dead wood. Also in wood structures.

The area around the nest mound is typically stripped of vegetation. Mature colonies average 3000 workers that agrressively defend the nest with stings and bites.

description:
In this observation I was able to find a compact Carpenter Ant. It belongs to the Kingdom Animalia and is further classified as a protosome. The size of this organism was about 0.5 cm to about 1 inch. It had distinctive circular body parts and a cylinder shaped back end of its body. The color of this organism was black. One characteristic present in the observation that defined its taxonomic group is its antlers and the insect's framework. The insect’s framework consisted of a distinct exoskeleton that is common for most insects and anthropods. Also, since this ant was also classified as an anthropod, it was a key indicator of its identification as a protosome since most protosomes are anthropods and insects. It is in a even more specific taxonomic group called a Formicidae. According to a Pests and insect control website, carpenter ants are ants that are attracted to decaying wood as this is a resource for their nest building. I found this in a grass field near my dorm which makes sense since our building is made out of wood. Carpenter ants don't live in a particular region. These insects usually live around indoor and outdoor areas that contain hollow or decaying wood.

Observation Description:
This organism is a Florida Carpenter Ant (Camponotus floridanus) and it belongs to the Kingdom Animalia. This organism was very small, about 3 cm in length. It had three body parts. These body parts were the head, thorax, and abdomen. Its head and thorax were red in color. The abdomen of the organism was black. The thorax was more thin and had an oval shape. The head was big and round, as well as the thorax. It had 2 antennae that were red. It walked very fast and had six long legs. The defining characteristics of this organism that allowed for the determination that it was a part of the Kingdom Animalia Protostomes, was that it had three body parts, three pairs of legs, and antennae. These are all characteristics of an insect, which are a part the protostomes. The Florida Carpenter ant is composed of several species. They are bicolored and they are the largest ants in Florida. According to the University of Florida, they have a ring of hair on their abdomen that’s round. They do not sting. They bite or release acid as a defense mechanism (Source: University of Florida).  

Location, Habitat, and Distribution: 
I found this organism at the University of South Florida by the chemistry building. It was 78 degrees and cloudy when I observed it. Lat: 28.061249 Lon: -82.414953. This organism covers four metropolitan areas of Florida. These areas are in Orlando, Daytona, Tampa Bay, and Sarasota-Ft. Myers (Source: University of Florida). They are distributed mainly in these areas of Florida. Their habitat consists of moist areas. They can live indoors or outdoors. You can find most of them in forests on wood. If they live indoors, they usually occupy the windows, roofs, or porches (Source: Wikipedia).

For reproduction, the ants undergo metamorphosis then forming a colony.  They have varying generation following the emergence of the queen.  This ant was found in a colony alongside a house with a cover over the colony, protecting the ants from any predators.  Usually, the ants prefer to nest in trees, under leads, in abandoned woody areas, any debris, or along wall voids. The geographic distribution of the Florida carpenter ant is all around the state of Florida, concentrated in Southeastern Florida especially.  They can also be found in Georgia and Alabama. description:
"Black carpenter ants are known to forage up to 100 yards or 91.4 metres (to one d.p.) in search of food. Workers are most active at night. They do establish chemical (pheromone) trails. The ants produce crackling sounds that can often be heard near a large nest. A large colony can contain thousands of individuals. The black carpenter ant does not sting, but the larger workers can administer a sharp bite, which can become further irritated by the injection of formic acid, which they produce. Workers tend aphids, with the smaller workers collecting honeydew and transferring it to larger workers that carry it back to the nest. In addition, foragers feed on dead insects and plant juices.

In their natural environment, carpenter ants nest in dead trees and other dead wood. This enhances decay, which has ecological benefits. However, the ant achieves pest status when a colony invades the wood of a house or other structure, damaging its structural integrity.[2]

Since they favor moist wood as a habitat, any condition that promotes moisture should be eliminated to prevent infestation. The easiest of these is keeping gutters clear so water does not run down the side of the structure or gain entry. Moist wood is much easier to chew. The ants do not eat the wood, but remove it to create galleries for their activities. The galleries run parallel to the grain, as they are created in the softer, nonlignin portions of the timber. The galleries have a sandpaper-like feel, due to fecal remnants, but the mud tubes produced by termiteswill not be present."

description:
The organism, Camponotus floridanus, is also called the Florida Carpenter Ant, and is a Protostome. This type of ant is native to the northern and central parts of Florida. This organism was found in Lettuce Lake Park in Tampa, Florida. This organism is likes to live in moist areas with decaying wood. The color of this ant is red and black. The length of these ants vary in size based on the gender. The males can be around 5-10 millimeters long while the females can be anywhere from 7-20 millimeters long because they are winged. These ants also are segmented organisms and have 12 segments. The way that these organisms reproduce is by having a queen who lays eggs and worker ants. The ants go through a metamorphosis from the time they are an egg, transitioning to a larvae, pupae, and then an adult.

These Florida Carpenter Ants were photographed at the University of South Florida campus on  a hot, sunny afternoon. It had segmented body, the whole body along with the long feet was reddish brown but the hind part was black. It was about 1.5 -2 cm long. According to http://entnemdept.ufl.edu/creatures/urban/ants/fl_carpenter_ants.htm , "The antennae of Florida carpenter ants are 12-segmented, with the terminal segment being slightly elongated and bullet-shaped, and without a club. There is a circular ring of hair at the end of the abdomen. The waist consists of one petiolar segment. The antennal scape is flattened basally and broad throughout. Workers vary in size, ranging from 5.5 to 11 mm in length. Smaller workers are called minors while larger workers are called majors. Winged females (alates) are the largest caste reaching up to 20 mm in length. There is no sting, but workers can bite and spray formic acid for defense. The thorax is evenly convex; a key characteristic of carpenter ants. The thorax and head are ash brown to rusty-orange and the gaster is black. Body hairs are abundant, long, and golden. Male reproductives are much smaller than queens with proportionally smaller heads and larger wings. Specific characters for C. floridanus include legs and antennal scapes with numerous long, coarse brown to golden erect hairs, shorter than those on the body. For C. tortuganus, specific characters include a major worker with head longer than broad; tibia of all legs and antennal scapes without erect hairs; and thinner than C. floridanus and paler with less color contrast."

description:
Description: This ant was approximately almost 1 centimeter in length. The ant had a black eye. The ant's head was red and it had antennae jutting out of its head. Its thorax was also a bright scarlet-red color, which matched the color of the ant's head. The abdomen, on the other hand, was a dark black color. The abdomen was larger in diameter than the thorax, but approximately the same length as the thorax. The head was slightly shorter than both the abdomen ad the thorax. The abdomen had two shallow ridges on it that divided it up into three sections. It also was pointed at the end. The ant had six legs that it used to maneuver itself through the branches and tree bark. The mandibles of the ant was slightly darker than the head, but it was also a red-black color.

Habitat: This observation took place on February 24th, 2020 at noon. The weather was almost 80 degrees Fahrenheit. The ant was found behind an oak tree that had a fallen trunk, so that the trunk was only three feet off the ground and horizontal. The ant was found in a shadier area of the tree that was also more moist. The shade came from the shadows of the foliage of surrounding trees. There were a lot of dead branches, as well as a lot of mosses where the ant was crawling. The habitat of this species is widespread, but they can be found in residential or woody areas (Gadau, Hoelldobler, and Schmid, 1996).

References: Gadau, J., Heinze, J., Hoelldobler, B., & Schmid, M. (1996). Population and colony structure of the carpenter ant Camponotus floridanus. Molecular Ecology, 5(6), 785-792.

The ant possessed six legs, two antennae, and its body was divided into three segments (head, thorax, abdomen) which were a brown/red color. Overall ants are protostomes meaning they possess true tissue, are bilaterally symmetrical, and develop the mouth before the anus in the embryonic stage.  Ants belong to the subphylum Hexapoda  which belongs to the phylum Arthropoda. Ants possess specific male or female characteristics and reproduce sexually.

This ant was found running up and down the length of a pole using its three pairs of legs, carrying particles  in a more sandy area surrounded by trees and dead foliage . description:
This is a Florida Carpenter ant, also known as the bull ant, and its scientific name is Camponotus floridanus. It was found on a sidewalk in a remote area in Clearwater near a pond. This ant was a reddish brown color with a robust and hairy black abdomen and a head that was disproportionately larger than the rest of its body. It had six legs with two antennae and was alone when the observation was made early morning at 6:50 in June 10th. It was also fairly large and compared to other common ants in Florida, it is a larger species. It belongs to the family formicidae, the genus Camponotus, and the phylum Arthopod which belongs to the clade of protostomes. This means that this ant has an exoskeleton structure, its embryonic development meant that the mouth forms first then the anus (opposite that of deuterostomes), and it's an invertebrate animal with a segmented body as it is an insect. This organism has many natural habitats all over Florida and can also be found along with its related species in the Americas and Europe. 

Reference: 
Warner, J. (2002, July). Featured Creatures. Retrieved June 12, 2020, from http://entnemdept.ufl.edu/creatures/urban/ants/fl_carpenter_ants.htm

Eastern Black Carpenter ants are most commonly found in woodlands, the age of forest and in suburban areas. They are about half and inch in length making them one of the larger ant species and are completely black. On their abdomen they also have yellowish hairs. They can be distinguished from the Hercules Ant because their jaw size is much less formidable. The life cycle of the Carpenter Ant begins as an egg that hatches into a larva that is taken care of the worker ants. The larvae then form into pupae which can form into an adult worker, a male with wings to start a new colony or an adult queen. Despite their name, Carpenter ants do not eat wood, but instead are secondary consumer eating and scavenging on other insects like earthworms. A potential predator of these ants could be  Fowler's toads, and an interesting competitor to these ants could be the Nine-Spotted Lady bug that feeds on aphids. The honeydew of the aphids is a common meal for Carpenter ants, and they have been known to protect them from predators.

description:
The Florida carpenter ant (Camponotus floridanus) is a species of carpenter ant native to Florida.
They come in a large variety of sizes depending on their class. They are typically a red to reddish-brown and have a black gaster.
Carpenter ants reside in moist, decayed woods. Unlike termites They do not eat wood, their diet consists of  many sweet things like insect honeydew and fruit juices. They will also eat insects.

These two ants are worker ants, indicated by their large heads. I was unable to measure their size but workers typically range from 8mm to 11mm. 
I was unable to locate their nest, but I assume it was near by as these were workers.

Fun fact about Florida Carpenter worker ants: they are able to spray formic acid as a defense mechanism.

description:
Visual Description: Ants are classed as protosomes. In these images, you can see Compact Carpenter Ants, a species that is native to Florida, specifically, the Sarasota, Tampa Bay area, Miami, and Florida Keys areas. These insects have a reddish/orange body with small hair-like structures throughout their exoskeleton. Towards the butt of the ant, more commonly known as the gaster, the coloration of the ant is a black tone. The ants vary in size ranging anywhere from 3mm to 6mm depending on the stage of life of the ant, whether it's young or fully grown. 

Defining Characteristics: The Compact Carpenter Ant is bullet-shaped, and has bodily hairs. These ants have no stinger and the thorax is evenly convex, which is a unique characteristic for ants. These ants feed on scale insects. One common misconception of these ants is that they eat wood. They do not. Rather, they remove wood in order to create galleries and tunnels for nesting. 

Habitats: Compact Carpenter Ants like to nest near moist, wooded areas, such as rivers, parks, ponds, lakes, and trees with holes, knots, or hollow cavities. Furthermore, they like to infest wood that is moist and rotten; therefore, they would love to live in areas of run-down wooden buildings such as abandoned homes and old wood sheds. 

Reference: Featured Creatures. UF, IFAS. https://entnemdept.ufl.edu/creatures/urban/ants/c_planatus.htm

Notes: This image was taken on October 12, 2021, at 5:54 p.m. At Cypress Point Park.

The organism was found outside Kosove Hall on USF campus, seen crawling across the concrete wall next to the wooden seating area, and was about 3 mm long. Compact carpenter ants also build their nests in places with hollow areas of usually wood. This ant is very distinctive because it has a red head and thorax, with a black gaster, “...the thorax is evenly convex is a characteristic of carpenter ants” (Warner). Compact carpenter ants are protostomes because they are bilaterally symmetric and develop their mouth before the anus during embryonic development. Ants like this reproduce in three ways, swarming, asexually, and budding, using eggs and sperm. The compact carpenter ant is “...now regarded as exotic to Florida, the compact carpenter ant occurs widely in Cuba and abundantly from Mexico to Colombia, and is well-established in Sarasota, Tampa, and east Miami and in the Florida Keys” (Warner). Compact carpenter ants thrive in temperate and subtropical climates.

description: At our home

This protostome is called a compact carpenter ant, and its scientific name is Camponotus planatus. He was observed at 12:20 pm on March 4, 2022. He was about a third of an inch long, so he was fairly small. His body shape consisted of what looked like three beads put together with some legs sticking off. His head resembled a rounded triangle, and it was a deep brown color. His torso looked similar in shape but more elongated and it was a red/brown color. He also had a circular end that was nearing black. He had six legs and two antennae. He was found in the urban habitat of a neighborhood cluster mailbox unit. At first, he was on one of the supporting beams, but then he made his way to the floor where he found some leaves and sticks to stand on. Description (size/shape/color): The compact carpenter ant is part of the Kingdom Animalia and family Formicidae. The carpenter ant is about 3-6 mm long in length and about 1mm wide in size and 1mm tall in height and has a red head and body with a black tail and red legs, and is sized to have narrow body, with a narrow head. The head and tail are circular shaped with a very narrow and thin elongated bullet-shaped body in between and 8 thin legs to the side. Their scientific name is Camponotus planatus.

Habitat: Compact Carpenter Ant are found in tropical areas. They often live in hollow logs and timbers of trees in warm forest areas, especially forest areas with damp wood, where the ants can build nests in and live in. They are also found near dead wood and grass culms. They are most common in sub-tropical Africa area and tropical areas in North America, especially southeastern United States.

Range: The compact carpenter ants primarily live in South Florida. It has recently become a pest in the south Florida region. They range from living in places all over Florida, such as Florida Keys, to also places such as Cuba, and some countries such as Columbia and Mexico. Within Florida, they can be found in many counties ranging from Sarasota to Miami, Florida Keys and Palm Beach county and surrounding areas. The ants in this observation were found in the Tampa area of South Florida, in the Lettuce Lake Park, which is a temperate forest area. Within the park, the ants were found in the sand. There was a lot of place near the lake where there is a lot of soil surrounded by grass. The ants dug up several holes in the soil to build their homes and were seen coming in and out of the hole in the soil and roaming around those holes, near the oak trees and the wooden tables built in the park shelter area.

Defining Characteristics of higher taxon: Carpenter ants are part of the Phylum Arthropoda, Kingdom Animalia, and Class Insecta, because they are protostomes which have a vertebrate and a metapleural gland which helps the ants fight off fungi and bacteria.

Visual Description: The two ants were sterile female worker ants as they do not have wings and were approximately 6 to 10 millimeters in size. The color of the ant is a deep red, brown, or black. It is noticeable that this species of worker ants do not have stingers. There is usually a circular ring of hairs at the end of the abdomen forming the acid pore. The thorax is evenly convex which is a key identifier for carpenter ants. 

Defining Characteristics:Ants are protostomes because the formation of the mouth occurs before the formation of the anus during embryo development, leading to a unique position of their organs. Worker carpenter ants are omnivorous and will attack live arthropods and scavenge on dead arthropods for proteins. Carpenter ants foraging in homes can be in search of sweets, moisture, or even new nesting sites, especially in kitchens, bathrooms, or other rooms that have water leaks from plumbing or around doors and windows.

Habitat:Camponotus plants or more commonly known as compact carpenter ants were sighted at USF Genshaft Dr. crawling up the Social Sciences building. The organism was observed in an urban environment. The worker ants were seeking to find a dry environment before afternoon showers. The forest is the carpenter ant’s natural habitat, any wet rotten wood attracts a new queen that may begin their own colony. 

Range:Carpenter ants are found throughout the world, occurring throughout the eastern United States and southeastern Canada. Two carpenter ant species that are common around structures in the South are the Florida carpenter ant and the Tortugas carpenter ant.

Additional Info:These bicolored arboreal ants are among the largest ants, making them appear as they forage or fly indoors and out. Carpenter ants have gotten their name because they excavate nests in wood, they are not like termites consuming the wood but find a home in the wood.
